name: C. S. Lewis

died.place: The Kilns, Headington Quarry, Oxford, England

life_summary: Clive Staples Lewis was born in Belfast in 1898. His mother died when he was nine, and he was then educated at boarding schools in England and privately by W. T. Kirkpatrick. He entered University College, Oxford, in 1917, was commissioned as an infantry officer and was wounded in France in April 1918; he resumed his Oxford studies in 1919 and took first-class honours in 1920, 1922 and 1923. From 1925 to 1954 he was Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen College, Oxford, and from 1930 he lived at The Kilns in Headington Quarry with Janie Moore and her daughter, joined in 1932 by his brother Warren. Having left Christianity in his youth, he became a theist (by his own dating in 1929, though Alister McGrath argues for 1930) and came to Christian belief in September 1931. During the Second World War he preached his first sermons in Oxford, spoke at RAF stations and gave four series of BBC talks that were later published as Mere Christianity; the Narnia books followed from 1950. In 1954 he was elected to a professorship at Cambridge, he married Joy Davidman in a civil ceremony in 1956 and a church ceremony in 1957, and she died in 1960; after a heart attack in July 1963 he resigned his chair and died at The Kilns that November.

phases.label: Belfast childhood and schooling
phases.summary: He grew up in Belfast. After his mother died in 1908 he attended Wynyard School, Campbell College, Cherbourg House and Malvern College, and from September 1914 he studied privately with W. T. Kirkpatrick until entering Oxford.

phases.label: Oxford entry and war service
phases.summary: He came up to University College, Oxford, in April 1917, was commissioned as an officer in September and was sent to France with the Somerset Light Infantry. He was wounded in April 1918, was discharged in December 1918 and resumed his Oxford studies in January 1919.

phases.label: Undergraduate and young tutor
phases.summary: As an undergraduate at University College he took firsts in 1920, 1922 and 1923, and from October 1924 he taught philosophy there as a temporary tutor. By 1921 at the latest he was sharing a household in Headington with Janie Moore and her daughter.

phases.label: Magdalen don, road to faith
phases.summary: He became Fellow and Tutor in English at Magdalen College, Oxford, in 1925 and met J. R. R. Tolkien in 1926. He became a theist (1929 by his own account, 1930 according to McGrath), his father died in 1929, he moved into The Kilns in 1930, and he came to Christian belief in September 1931.

phases.label: Early Christian years at Magdalen
phases.summary: Now a practising Anglican layman, he continued teaching at Magdalen and lived at The Kilns, where his brother Warren joined the household in 1932. The Inklings began meeting around him from about 1933, and he published The Allegory of Love (1936) and Out of the Silent Planet (1938).
phases.place: Oxford (Magdalen College; The Kilns, Headington Quarry)

phases.label: Wartime preacher and broadcaster
phases.summary: While still a Magdalen tutor, he preached his first sermons at the University Church of St Mary the Virgin and elsewhere, visited RAF stations to speak (1941–1943) and gave four series of BBC radio talks between 1941 and 1944. He was the first president of the Oxford University Socratic Club from 1942 and published The Screwtape Letters as a book in 1942.

phases.label: Late Magdalen years, Narnia
phases.summary: He remained a tutor at Magdalen, preached 'Miserable Offenders' in 1946 at Headington Quarry and Northampton, published the first Narnia books from 1950 and Mere Christianity in 1952. Janie Moore died in 1951, and in September 1952 he met Joy Davidman, who had been writing to him since January 1950.

phases.label: Cambridge chair and marriage
phases.summary: Elected Professor of Medieval and Renaissance English at Cambridge and a fellow of Magdalene College in 1954, he took up his duties in January 1955, spending term weeks in Cambridge and returning to The Kilns in Oxford. He married Joy Davidman in 1956 (civil) and 1957 (church), was widowed in 1960, resigned in August 1963 after a heart attack and died at The Kilns.

corrections: Father's death: the biographer gave 25 September 1929 as certain, but Hooper's chronology (C.S. Lewis Institute) and the C.S. Lewis Foundation give 24 September while the Tour Guide gives 25 September; changed to date_iso 1929-09 and noted that sources differ.

Mrs Moore household: 'from 1921' was stated as certain, but the Headington history site places the Headington household from 1919, while the Institute has Lewis moving in with them in June 1921; the phase now says 'by 1921 at the latest', and the Moore death event now says 'for about three decades'.
Magdalene College, Cambridge: the phase said he was a fellow 'from 1955'; changed to elected in 1954 (Magdalen College blog, Wikipedia), taking up duties January 1955 (Institute).
Cambridge election event: made the date more precise, from June 1954 to 4 June 1954 (Tour Guide timeline). Replaced the Magdalen blog, which gives only the year, with the Institute chronology.
War service phase: added his December 1918 discharge (Institute), and the Somerset Light Infantry unit is now cited to the Tour Guide timeline.
Wounded event: added 'during the Battle of Arras' (Foundation and Tour Guide), and replaced the Foundation citation with the Tour Guide timeline, which names the unit.
Transposition event: the biographer's 'Whit Sunday' is now 'Feast of Pentecost', the wording of the cited CSLewis.com page.
BBC talks event: replaced the C.S. Lewis Foundation citation, which does not give 6 August, with the CSLewis.com 'Anniversary of Lewis's First Broadcast Talk' page, which confirms 6 August 1941.
Socratic Club event: replaced the Wikipedia citation with the Hooper chronology (C.S. Lewis Institute), which gives 26 January 1942.
Wartime phase: specified that his RAF talks ran 1941–1943 (Wikipedia) and added Wikipedia as a source; 'Screwtape' is now described as published as a book in 1942 (it had been serialised in 1941).

Whipsnade event: replaced the C.S. Lewis Institute 'His Life and Works' citation, which gives no date, with Christian History Institute; the 28 September 1931 date is still supported by the Tour Guide Addison's Walk page.
Janie Moore death event: kept 12 January 1951 (Headington and Foundation agree).
Heart attack event: kept 15 July 1963 as given by Crossway (Wikipedia says 16 July); reworded to say he received last rites on 16 July.
Resignation event: replaced the C.S. Lewis Foundation citation, which does not mention the resignation, with Wikipedia; Crossway dates it to mid-August 1963.

Bedside marriage: kept 21 March 1957 (Headington history, Joy Davidman portrait, Tour Guide, Wikipedia). The Foundation and Institute chronologies give December 1956 instead; this conflict is noted here, not in the event.
Civil marriage event: replaced the Joy Davidman portrait citation with the Institute chronology, which gives the exact date of 23 April 1956.
Joy Davidman correspondence: made it more precise, from 'since 1950' to 'since January 1950' (C.S. Lewis Institute portrait).

Early Christian years phase: added publication years for The Allegory of Love (1936) and Out of the Silent Planet (1938) from EBSCO, and changed Inklings to 'from about 1933' because the Tour Guide dates regular Thursday meetings from 1940.
Late Magdalen phase: added his 1946 sermon 'Miserable Offenders' at Headington Quarry and Northampton (CSLewis.com Lewis as Preacher), which is relevant to the sermon library.
Death event: made clear that the funeral at Holy Trinity was on 26 November (Crossway) and that burial was in the churchyard (Headington history).
Belfast schooling phase: added Kirkpatrick's location (Great Bookham) to place, and dated the start of his tutoring to September 1914 (Foundation: 19 September 1914).
Life summary: made the Warren move-in year (1932) and the civil/church marriage years (1956/1957) explicit, and rephrased the wartime sentence to match the verified RAF and BBC details.
